Q: Large contour not found in binary image A:

Here is a slightly shorter method to find the largest contour in Python OpenCV. It sorts on area and finds the max area.

  • Read the input

  • Invert the input so you have bright objects on black background

  • Convert to grayscale

  • Otsu threshold

  • Get contours and directly get the largest contour

  • Draw the biggest contour in red on a copy of the input

  • Save the results

Input image:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# read image
img = cv2.imread('oval.png')

# invert img so white objects on black background
img2 = 255 - img

# convert to grayscale
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img2,cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# threshold
thresh = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY+cv2.THRESH_OTSU)[1]

# get largest contour
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]
big_contour = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

# draw red contour on copy of input
result = img.copy()
cv2.drawContours(result, [big_contour], 0, (0,0,255), 2)

# save resulting images
cv2.imwrite('oval_thresh.png',thresh)
cv2.imwrite('oval_results.png',result)
    
# show thresh and result    
cv2.imshow("thresh", thresh)
cv2.imshow("result", result)
cv2.waitKey(0)
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

Q: How to create smooth interpolations between two images with OpenCV? A:

I won't go into rotating the homograph, but here is one way to warp the one image onto the other using ORB and perspective warp in Python OpenCV.

(An affine warp may be sufficient. But I did not know if there was any slight perspective distortions to either image)

  • Read the two images

  • Convert them to grayscale

  • Use ORB to get keypoints and descriptors

  • Match the features using with a Brute Force Matcher and Hamming distance

  • Sort the match by distance so best match is first

  • Keep only the top 50 matches

  • Make sure there are enough good matches

  • Find the homography

  • Warp img2 to match img2

  • Save the warped image

  • Define a delay and show alternating images until a key is pressed on the keyboard

Reference image (img1):

Image to be warped (img2):

import cv2
import numpy as np

# Load the images
img1 = cv2.imread('top_view1.jpg')  # Reference i.e., Destination image
img2 = cv2.imread('top_view2.jpg')  # Image to be warped to match reference image

# Convert the images to graysccale
gray1 = cv2.cvtColor(img1, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
gray2 = cv2.cvtColor(img2, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# Detect keypoints and descriptors using ORB
orb = cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=1000)
keypoints1, descriptors1 = orb.detectAndCompute(gray1, None)
keypoints2, descriptors2 = orb.detectAndCompute(gray2, None)

# Match features using Brute-Force Matcher with Hamming distance
bf = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_HAMMING, crossCheck=True)
matches = bf.match(descriptors1, descriptors2)

# Sort matches by distance (best matches first)
matches = sorted(matches, key=lambda x: x.distance)

# Keep only the top matches
good_matches = matches[:50]

# Make sure there are enough matches to calculate homography
if len(good_matches) > 10:
    # Extract location of matching points
    # Note: queryIdx is img1 (destination), trainIdx is img2 (source)
    dst_pts = np.float32([keypoints1[m.queryIdx].pt for m in good_matches]).reshape(-1, 1, 2)
    src_pts = np.float32([keypoints2[m.trainIdx].pt for m in good_matches]).reshape(-1, 1, 2)

    # Find the homography matrix using RANSAC
    H, mask = cv2.findHomography(src_pts, dst_pts, cv2.RANSAC, 5.0)

    # Warp img2 to match img1 via perspective
    height, width, channels = img1.shape
    img2_warped = cv2.warpPerspective(img2, H, (width, height))

    # Save result
    cv2.imwrite('warped_image2_orb.jpg', img2_warped)
    
    # show results
    # Define delay in milliseconds (e.g., 500ms = 0.5 seconds per image)
    delay_ms = 500

    print("Displaying alternating images. Press any key on your keyboard to exit")

    # Keep track of which image to show
    show_flag = True

    while True:
        # Select which image to display
        current_image = img1 if show_flag else img2_warped
        window_name = "Image Comparison"
        cv2.imshow(window_name, current_image)
    
        # Wait until a key is pressed (then it returns a key code (> -1))
        key = cv2.waitKey(delay_ms)
    
        if key != -1:
            # A key was pressed, so break the loop
            break
        
        # Toggle the boolean flag for the next iteration
        show_flag = not show_flag

    cv2.destroyAllWindows()

else:
    print("Not enough good matching points found")

Q: Override equals but still have reference equality check A:

I understood OP's question as: "I have overriden __eq__ in two instances a and b and wish to compare a == b without invoking the custom dunder."

If that is the case; for example, you have:

class Foo:
    def __init__(self, val: int):
        self.val = val
    def __eq__(self, other):
        # override logic, e.g. consider two instances equal
        # if they have the same `val`
        return isinstance(other, type(self)) and self.val == other.val

a = Foo(42)
b = Foo(42)

You can perform a "reference" comparison using object.__eq__(a, b). EDIT: I realised that object.__eq__ returns NotImplemented; it's probably best to follow the other answers and use a is b instead, as that is what == does under the hood when it can't find a custom __eq__.

Q: Cross-platform command to activate venv A:

If you actually look at what the activate scripts do, they are just putting the <venv>/bin directory first on the PATH so that the stuff in the venv is found before system pythons/etc on standard PATH.

I would guess on windows it is the same, but you would need to read the windows activate script to check if it is doing anything more than setting the PATH.

Personally I find the idea of needing to remember to activate/deactivate venv super annoying.

Instead, anytime we need a global python script installed somewhere with any dependencies (now requires venv)...we just have our project file(s) and optionally a requirements file. Then we setup the venv in the project dir (installing deps if we have a requirements.txt file)...and then add a wrapper script to manage running our python script so we don't need to think about venv.

setting up venv in project dir

(Note: This bash script is to illustrate how we setup the venv but of course you can do this any way you want or have one "install" script for nix and another for windows.)

#!/bin/bash

PROJ_DIR="/path/to/project"
PYTHON_VER="python3.14"
VENV_DIR=".venv"

# go to project dir
pushd "$PROJ_DIR"

# setup the venv
"$PYTHON_VER" -m venv "$VENV_DIR"

# install requirements.txt in venv if we have them
# putting the venv on the PATH here ensures we run the right pip/python and 
# put the deps in the venv...without needing to `activate`
test -f requirements.txt && PATH="$VENV_DIR/bin:$PATH" pip install -r requirements.txt

popd

wrapper script

can look something like this. you can make one wrapper for windows and another wrapper for linux but they both do the same thing... they put the venv on the path and forward the arguments to the python script and return the same exit code as the python script.

For convenience we like to name this script the same as out python entry script but minus the .py so we can avoid needing to template a script name into this file.

#!/bin/bash

PYSCRIPT_NAME="$0.py"  #e.g. this file is my-script and our python file is my-script.py

CWD="$(dirname "$0")"
PATH="$CWD/.venv/bin:$PATH"

"$CWD/.venv/bin/python" "$PYSCRIPT_NAME" "$@"

exit $?

Then you can invoke the wrapper script from ANY path on your system without calling activating a venv and everything will work.

If you build a similar wrapper for windows then you are set. Someone/CI just needs to know whether they are windows or linux and then invoke the right entry point based on that. (e.g. .sh file vs .cmd file).

Q: Selenium Test opens the Chrome window in headless mode A:

Since Selenium v4.11.0, all the selenium4 bindings includes Selenium Manager which is a command-line tool implemented in Rust that provides automated driver and browser management for Selenium. Selenium bindings use this tool by default so you do not need to download it of use webdrivermanager to download any binaries or add anything to your code or do anything else to use it.

As you are using the maven dependency of Selenium v4.35.0, the in-built Selenium Manager will automatically take care of discovering, downloading, and cacheing the drivers required by Selenium when these drivers are unavailable.

So you can safely remove the WebDriverManager dependency.

Update

Corey Goldberg's answer points us to the discussion in SeleniumHQ chromium/chromedriver 150.0.7871.46-1~deb13u1: Chrome instance exits on startup.

Solution

The solution will be to downgrade google-chrome to previous version i.e. v149.x
